title: Integer Types, Ranges and Signedness
learningObjectives: Identify signed and unsigned integer types and inspect their limits.
Explain the modulo behavior of unsigned integer arithmetic.
Recognize that signed integer overflow is undefined behavior.
Apply safe comparisons and loop conditions when signed and unsigned values interact.
Choose an integer type that can represent the required domain and intermediate results.

understand.concept: C integer types include _Bool, char, short, int, long and long long, with signed and unsigned forms where permitted. Their ranges depend on implementation characteristics. Unsigned arithmetic is reduced modulo one more than the maximum representable value. Signed overflow is undefined behavior. Integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions can change the type used in an expression.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct integer type requires considering range, arithmetic behaviour and interfaces. Signedness bugs can affect comparisons, loops, array indexing and input validation.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Signed and unsigned values

Signed integer types represent negative and nonnegative values. Unsigned integer types represent only nonnegative values and have a range determined by their width. Use limits from `<limits.h>` rather than assuming a particular range.

## 2. Unsigned wraparound

Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo one more than the maximum value. For example, subtracting one from an unsigned zero produces the maximum value of that unsigned type. This behavior is defined, but accidental wraparound can still be a logic or security defect.

## 3. Signed overflow

If a signed arithmetic operation produces a value outside the representable range, behavior is undefined. Do not rely on a signed integer wrapping from its maximum to its minimum. Check bounds before performing the operation.

## 4. Mixed signedness

When signed and unsigned operands are combined, integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions determine a common type. A negative signed value can be converted to a large unsigned value, producing surprising comparisons. Avoid mixing signed and unsigned values without a clear reason.

## 5. Safer arithmetic

Check addition and multiplication bounds before computing them, use an appropriate wider or unsigned type when justified, and validate external input before conversion. Compiler warnings can help reveal suspicious signedness conversions.

examples.title: A second case
examples.code: int maximum = INT_MAX;\n/* Do not compute maximum + 1 in signed int. */\nprintf("%d\\n", maximum);
examples.explanation: Adding one to INT_MAX in signed int would overflow and has undefined behaviour; use a wider or otherwise suitable representation after checking its range.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small C program that demonstrates the central rules in CL2.6. Compile with warnings enabled, run it with ordinary and boundary values, and explain each result in your own words.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL2.6 using different values and names. Include one likely mistake as a separate experiment, observe the compiler diagnostic or behavior, then correct it. Record the rule that explains the correction.
hints: Start by identifying the exact type of every object and expression.
Check the C language rule before assuming a platform-specific result.
Use compiler warnings as feedback, not as proof of correctness.
Test normal values and important boundaries.
Explain why the result follows from the language rules.

questions.prompt: What happens when unsigned arithmetic exceeds its maximum value?
options: The result is reduced modulo one more than the maximum representable value
The value becomes a negative number
questions.answer: The result is reduced modulo one more than the maximum representable value
questions.explanation: Unsigned integer arithmetic has defined modulo behavior.

questions.prompt: What is the result of signed integer overflow in C?
questions.explanation: C does not define signed overflow as wraparound.

questions.prompt: Why can comparing a negative int with an unsigned value be surprising?
options: The usual arithmetic conversions may convert the negative value to unsigned
The compiler always changes both to double
questions.answer: The usual arithmetic conversions may convert the negative value to unsigned
questions.explanation: Mixed signedness can change the common type used by the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which header provides INT_MAX and UINT_MAX?
questions.explanation: The limits.h header provides integer type limits.

questions.prompt: What is a safer approach before adding two signed integers?
options: Check whether the result would exceed the representable range
questions.answer: Check whether the result would exceed the representable range
questions.explanation: The program must prevent an out-of-range signed operation before evaluating it.
